archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A thick-framed, strong-armed quarterback whose real value comes when the pocket breaks down and he runs, while his passing from the pocket is still uneven: shaky accuracy, slow processing and a long history of taking sacks.

report.headline: Scrambles keep him afloat; sacks and misses keep him below average.
report.take:
Malik Willis is finally getting a real starter's sample, and it looks a lot more like his 2022 Titans tape than the two short, efficient Green Bay cameos that earned him this job. Through seven starts his passing EPA per dropback is -0.071 (32nd of 47), his CPOE is -5.81 (41st) and his sack rate is 10.3% (41st). Those are bottom-third passing numbers in an offense that already runs far more than the situation calls for: its pass rate over expected of -9.6 ranks 31st. The 2024-25 Packers lines (CPOE of 6.9 and then 22, yards per attempt of 10.19 and then 12.06) came on two or three games each with a far better supporting cast. They were never likely to hold, and they haven't.

The legs are what make him playable. His 22 scrambles have gained 204 yards and 12 first downs at 0.897 EPA apiece. That is why his dropbacks as a whole add up to +1.8 EPA even though his passes alone sit at -14.4. Designed runs are a different story: 1.92 yards a carry and a 33% stuff rate. His rushing value is improvisation, not the read-option game. As a thrower the profile splits sharply by depth. In the 10-19 yard window he is genuinely good (0.435 EPA per attempt), and short throws are fine. Screens and dump-offs behind the line have cost -11.2 EPA, though, and the deep ball connects only 24.2% of the time.

The sacks are not new. His pressure-to-sack rate was 0.435 in 2022, 0.667 in 2024 and 0.6 in 2025, and this year's 32% (27th of 38) is actually his best. He holds the ball (3.06-second time to throw) hunting for the off-script play, and the bill comes due on third down: 8 sacks on 59 plays and a 39% conversion rate. The 5 fumbles charted as turnover-worthy, 3 of them lost (43rd of 47), come from the same habit of holding on.

The last three games are the hopeful part. His EPA per dropback is 0.034, right at league average, his CPOE is -1.3, and the touchdown rate has jumped to 6.3%. He went turnover-free with no bad throws against the Jets, and his best CPOE of the year (2.3) came against New England. Part of that is softer defenses after a stretch that included the league's top unit in Minnesota. Part of it is a tighter, shorter plan, with an aggressiveness of 3.1% against the Patriots. The sacks (11.1%) and interceptions (3.8%) have not improved, so call this a better floor rather than a breakout.

strengths.title: Scrambling turns broken plays positive
strengths.body: When the pocket collapses he is a real threat. Scrambles produce chunk gains and first downs at an EPA rate far above anything he does as a passer. This is a stable trait: he has ranked in the top 30 of rushing yards every career season despite tiny samples, and he is 3rd this year. It also props up his fantasy floor.

strengths.title: Intermediate window is a weapon
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards are the most productive part of his game: high EPA, a 51.5% success rate, and CPOE near neutral. His arm plays well over the middle when he has time to set. It's a 33-attempt sample, but it matches the efficiency of his best Packers outings.

strengths.title: Tight end connection with Dulcich
strengths.body: Greg Dulcich has been his most efficient high-volume target, and Caleb Douglas has produced on fewer looks. Malik Washington gets the most volume at a modest rate. When the ball goes to the tight end and the outside vertical option, the passing game works.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career-long trait
concerns.body: His 10.3% sack rate ranks near the bottom, and every prior season showed an even worse pressure-to-sack rate. That makes it who he is, not bad luck. Some of it is the cost of hunting scrambles, but the drives that die on third-down sacks aren't fully paid back by the 22 scrambles.

concerns.title: Accuracy lags expectation
concerns.body: A -5.81 CPOE and a 13.1% bad-throw rate say he misses throws he should complete. Deep balls land only about a quarter of the time, and his screen game is negative. The recent CPOE gain is real but covers only three games, and it came partly from shortening the throws.

concerns.title: Ball security when holding it
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank 43rd of 47. Five charted turnover-worthy fumbles suggest that isn't just bad bounces; it is the price of extending plays in traffic. Expect the fumbles to continue at some rate as long as he plays this style.

trend.note: The first five games, including a -12.4 EPA game against top-ranked Minnesota, were rough. His last two have been his best as a passer. Over the last three his EPA per dropback climbed to league average, though sacks and interceptions held steady.

nextGame.headline: Leaky Lions secondary meets a shootout script, minus his tackle
nextGame.body:
Detroit's pass defense ranks 29th in EPA, is 28th against deep throws and 27th against short ones, and gives up more fantasy points to quarterbacks than anyone. Its offense ranks 3rd in pass EPA, while Miami's pass defense is dead last. With Miami a 7-point home underdog and a 50.5 total, the likely script has Willis trailing and throwing more than this run-first offense normally allows. Detroit is also a pass funnel (5.6 points over normal, 3rd). The catch is the rush: Detroit's hit rate ranks 5th and its sack rate 7th, which is exactly the pressure that has stalled him all year.

Availability tilts both ways. Miami is without left tackle Kadyn Proctor (concussion, out), a 100%-snap starter. That makes the sack problem worse and may push the plan even quicker and shorter. Detroit's back seven is thin: Kerby Joseph is out, Brian Branch (concussion) and D.J. Reed (hip) are questionable, and linebacker Jack Campbell, a 97%-snap player, is doubtful with a neck injury. Losing Campbell softens the middle of the field where Dulcich and the intermediate throws live, and it removes a natural spy against his scrambles.

keyMatchups.title: Detroit pass rush vs. backup tackle
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gets home often, and Willis converts pressure into sacks at a career-long rate. With Proctor out, this decides whether the offense stays on schedule. Expect quick game and moving pockets.

keyMatchups.title: Dulcich against a soft TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Detroit has let top tight ends score well over their averages and sends an above-league share of targets to the position. Dulcich is Willis's most efficient volume target, and a possible Campbell absence opens the seams further.

keyMatchups.title: Trailing script forces volume
keyMatchups.body: Miami's defense can't stop the pass and Detroit's offense is top five, so Willis will likely throw from behind. His trailing-by-9+ numbers are closer to neutral than his one-score play, which helps volume-driven fantasy output more than it helps his efficiency.

nextGame.watch: How many sacks he takes in the first half without Proctor. If he stays clean, the Detroit secondary is there to be hit.

restOfSeason.body:
The rushing floor is the sustainable part: scrambling has been his calling card in every stop, and the volume of 5-6 carries a game should hold. The passing should settle around the recent version, roughly league-average efficiency on dropbacks with modest volume in a run-first offense. His 6.3% touchdown rate over the last three games will likely drift back toward his season level. The sacks won't vanish; they have followed him through three teams. Expect something in the range of 165-225 passing yards, 0.8-1.5 passing touchdowns and 25-45 rushing yards a game. The variance will come mostly from game script and turnovers.

The defense behind him is the swing in both directions. A pass defense ranked last keeps forcing shootouts, which props up his volume even when his efficiency lags. The ceiling is capped by an offense that wants to run, and the floor is threatened by fumbles and interceptions that haven't improved.
swingFactors: Offensive line health, starting with Proctor's return
Whether the recent accuracy gains hold up against better defenses
Game script driven by Miami's last-ranked pass defense

confidence.note: Seven starts is a real sample, and the sack and accuracy traits match his career. The recent improvement covers only three games, against middling defenses.
